info.bio:
The KLF fue una banda inglesa originaria de Londres durante finales de los 80 y principios de los 90. Sus miembros eran dos hombres de experiencia y trayectoria musical, el músico inglés Jimmy Cauty y Bill Drummond, músico, cantante y compositor originario de Escocia.
Sus estilos musicales son el techno, dance y acid house.
También fueron conocidos mundialmente como The Justified Ancients of Mu Mu (The JAMs) y The Timelords. Dichos nombres tomados

scenes.name: Madchester y ambient house
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Un movimiento de Manchester que marca la música de baile como ningún otro de los ochenta: la fusión de psicodelia, techno y pop. KLF importa el acid house; los Stone Roses mezclan ritmos disco hipnóticos, melodías pegadizas y entusiasmo sesentero; los Happy Mondays de Shaun Ryder (Bummed) y Black Grape; Charlatans, Nitzer Ebb, Shamen, Pop Will Eat Itself, Jesus Jones. Más allá de la moda, 808 State (herederos de Kraftwerk, «Pacific State»), William Orbit, Richard Kirk, A Guy Called Gerald, el collage de Coldcut y Primal Scream (Screamadelica).
scenes.family: Soul, funk, disco, hip hop y baile

scenes.name: Ambient house e IDM
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Música para relajarse en las «chill-out rooms» que se convierte en género propio, entre el techno y el minimalismo: Chill Out de KLF es su manifiesto; Irresistible Force, Orb (Adventures Beyond The Ultraworld, U.F. Orb: el DJ convertido en compositor clásico), Ultramarine, Global Communication, Spacetime Continuum, Banco De Gaia, Woob. La «Intelligent Dance Music»: Orbital (Brown Album), Eat Static, Sabres Of Paradise, Future Sound Of London, Black Dog, Leftfield, Richard James / Aphex Twin, Plastikman, Moby, Vapourspace. Y la música de baile para no bailarines: Scanner, Faithless, Lo-Fidelity Allstars, Luke Slater, Christian Vogel, David Holmes, Susumu Yokota.

podcast.title: Formation as The Justified Ancients of Mu Mu (1987)
podcast.body: Bill Drummond and Jimmy Cauty first appeared in 1987 under the name The Justified Ancients of Mu Mu, or The Jams. "They first appeared in 1987 under the name The Justified Agents of Moo Moo."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: "Children, We Love You" Rave Stunt (1989)
podcast.body: During a rave performance in 1989, The KLF engaged in unusual behavior by throwing £1000 worth of pound notes into the crowd, with each note featuring the message "Children, We Love You." "During one performance at a rave in 1989, they threw a thousand pounds worth of pound notes at the crowd with each one featuring the message, Children, We Love You."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Global Singles Success (1991)
podcast.body: By 1991, The KLF had become one of the biggest selling singles acts in the world, primarily through their 12-inch single releases. "More records followed, largely in the form of 12-inch singles. And in 1991, the KLF was one of the biggest selling singles acts in the world."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: 1992 Brit Awards Controversy
podcast.body: At the 1992 Brit Awards, The KLF planned extreme stunts, including dumping buckets of blood over the audience and disemboweling a dead sheep on stage, which organizers prohibited. Drummond then threatened to cut off his own hand with an axe, but instead fired blanks over the audience with a machine gun. The purchased sheep was later dumped at an after-party, and their Best Artist trophy was found buried near Stonehenge. "At the 1992 Brit Awards, they plan to dump buckets of blood over the audience and to disembowel a dead sheep on stage. And organizers wouldn't allow that. Drummond said, fight! I'll just cut my hand off with an axon stage. That didn't happen, thankfully. Instead, Drummond showed up with a machine gun and fired blanks over the head of the audience. The sheep, which had already been purchased, was dumped at an after-party. The best artist trophy they won that night was later found buried near Stonehenge."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: The K Foundation and Money Burning (1993-1994)
podcast.body: In 1993, Drummond and Cauty formed The K Foundation, mounting various exhibitions. Their most famous act occurred on August 23, 1994, when they burned their remaining £1 million in front of the press on the Scottish Isle of Jura, filming the entire event. "That they weren't done. In 1993, Drummond and Coddy formed the K Foundation, which mounted some interesting exhibitions. The most famous happened on August 23, 1994, when they took whatever money they had left, which was about a million pounds, and burned the money in front of the press on the Scottish aisle of Jura. They filmed everything, too."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Burned One Million Pounds in Cash – Jura, Scotland, August 23, 1994
podcast.body: After a series of deliberately provocative stunts (including dumping a dead sheep and eight gallons of blood at an awards show after-party) and announcing their retirement from music until world peace was achieved, Bill Drummond and Jimmy Cauty of the KLF deleted their entire back catalogue and made what is believed to be the single largest cash withdrawal in UK banking history. They nailed one million pounds in £50 notes to a board, paraded it around England as an artwork called *Nailed to the Wall*, then on the evening of August 23, 1994, traveled to the island of Jura in Scotland with one journalist and one cameraman. In an abandoned boathouse, they set fire to the entire million pounds. A documentary called *Watch the KLF Foundation Burn a Million Quid* exists on YouTube. The pair have never fully explained their motivation beyond vague references to satire of materialism and contempt for the music industry. "They deliberately burned one million pounds of their own money."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Public Money Burning (1994)
podcast.body: The KLF is known as one of the most subversive experimental bands in British music history, notably for publicly burning one million pounds in cash in 1994. "Remember that this is a band that burned a million pounds in cash in public"

podcast.body: The KLF conceived of building a pyramid constructed from the remains of 34,592 deceased individuals. Construction on this "People's Pyramid" began on November 23rd, 2018, in the Liverpool area, with individuals able to reserve a spot for 99 pounds. "came up with the idea of building a pyramid made of the remains of 34,592 dead people."

podcast.title: "Copyright Liberation Front" Name Origin
podcast.body: The name KLF is an acronym for "Copyright Liberation Front," reflecting the group's attitude and approach towards intellectual property and sampling in their music. This philosophy influenced their production methods and contributed to the controversies surrounding some of their releases. "After all, KLF stands for Copyright Liberation Front."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Album Cover Inspiration and Intent
podcast.body: The cover art for The KLF's album *Chill Out* was directly inspired by Pink Floyd's *Atom Heart Mother*. According to Bill Drummond, this was intended as a mockery of progressive rock, a genre they considered pretentious. Despite this satirical intent, the album itself went on to become a cult classic in electronic music. "su portada está directamente inspirada en el Atom Gersmoder de Pink Floyd. Según Drummond era una burlal, rock progresivo que ellos consideraban pretencioso y, lónicamente, el disco se volvió un clásico de cultón de música electrónica."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: Chill Out: La pausa que necesitaba la electrónica

podcast.title: Bill Drummond's Background
podcast.body: Bill Drummond previously managed Echo and the Bunnyman in their early days and founded Zoo Records. In 1986, at age 33 and 1/3, he declared he was quitting all music industry jobs to do something revolutionary, initially writing books before deciding hip hop was the future and forming The Jams with Cauty. "Drummond used to be the manager of Echo and the Bunnyman in the early days, and was the founder of a label called Zoo Records. In 1986, Drummond declared that he was quitting all the jobs in the music industry because he turned 33 and 1, 30 years old and now needed to do something revolutionary. He started writing books before deciding that hip hop was the future. He called up Coddy and the Justified Agents of Moo Moo, or Jams, was formed in 1987."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Building a Pyramid from Human Ashes
podcast.body: The KLF, a distinctive music and art collective, is engaged in a project to construct a pyramid in Liverpool using the cremated remains of 34,592 deceased individuals. People can have their ashes formed into a brick to be added to this structure, with a reservation cost of £99. "The KLF, the weird music and art collective, is building a pyramid out of thirty four thousand five hundred ninety two dead people."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Copyright Liberation Front Philosophy
podcast.body: The KLF, also known as "The Timelords" for specific projects, adopted the moniker "Copyright Liberation Front," reflecting their stance on sampling and copyright, which sometimes led to issues with the availability of their music. "After all, KLF stands for Copyright Liberation Front."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Jimmy Cauty's Background
podcast.body: Jimmy Cauty was the guitarist in a band called Brilliant, which was also managed by Bill Drummond. "Coddy was the guitarist and a band called Brilliant, who was also managed by Drummond."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Live Recording in One Take
podcast.body: The KLF's seminal album *Chill Out* was recorded live in a single take, a remarkable feat that contributes to its flowing and immersive narrative style. This recording method enhanced the album's natural, unedited feel, crucial for its ambient design. "Como curiosidad, se grabó un directo en una sola toma."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: Chill Out: La pausa que necesitaba la electrónica

podcast.title: Origin of "Ambient House" Term
podcast.body: Jimmy Cauty, along with Bill Drummond, began referring to their productions, which were inspired by the relaxing sessions at "The White Room," as "ambient House." This term was an early designation for the evolving sound that would later be known as Chill Out. "Fue un Jimmy Couty junto a Bill Drummond, quien estenía en el otro grupo seminal del género de KLF, quienes, a sus producciones inspiradas en esas sisiones, empezaron a llamarlas ambient House."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: Chill Out: La pausa que necesitaba la electrónica

podcast.title: Pioneers of Ambient House
podcast.body: This artist (likely KLF), along with The Orp (The Orb), was instrumental in initiating Ambient House and the concept of chill-out rooms, which offered atmospheric passages in electronic music. However, these spaces were still largely considered extensions of the dance floor, serving as temporary respites for conversation and recharging rather than dedicated deep listening. "incluso los pasajes más atmosféricos del Ambient House o las chill-out rooms que habían iniciado KLSE o The Orp, sigan siendo extensiones de la pista."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: Qué fue el IDM y por qué cambió la música electrónica

podcast.title: Retirement and Record Deletion
podcast.body: Following the 1992 Brit Awards, The KLF declared their grand retirement from the music industry and immediately deleted all their records. "That was their grand retirement from the music industry, and they immediately deleted all their records."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Sampling Practices
podcast.body: The KLF, whose name stands for Copyright Liberation Front, were known for not being keen on clearing samples in their music. This approach to sampling led to some of their tracks being unavailable on mainstream platforms. "And second, the KLF were never really keen on clearing samples."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: The People's Pyramid Plan
podcast.body: Exactly 23 years after burning the money, The KLF announced a new plan called The People's Pyramid, which will be constructed using bricks, each containing 23 grams of human ashes. The complete pyramid is planned to have 34,592 bricks, with a registration cost of £99 to secure a place, requiring individuals to arrange for 23 grams of their ashes to be sent after death. "Only 23 years to the day after they burned all that money, they announced a new plan called the People's Pyramid, using bricks, each containing 23 grams of human ashes. When complete, this pyramid will have a total of 34,592 bricks. If you would like to secure your place in the pyramid, it'll cost you 99 pounds to register, and then of course you have to find somebody to send them 23 grams of your ashes after you die."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Transformation into The Timelords and KLF
podcast.body: After The Jams, they resurfaced as The Timelords, releasing a Doctor Who-themed hit that sampled Gary Glitter's "Rock and Roll Part 2," and subsequently morphed into The KLF. "They resurfaced under the name of the Timelords, who released a Doctor Who themed hit that made the use of the Gary Glitter song Rock and Roll Part 2, and from there they morphed into the KLF."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Unauthorized Sampling Controversies
podcast.body: The Jams immediately caused problems by using unauthorized samples from artists like The Beatles and Abba, leading to legal issues. They traveled to Sweden to negotiate with Abba, and upon failure, burned the remaining offending records in a field and threw others into the North Sea. They continued to infringe copyrights, including Whitney Houston's material, before The Jams ended. "He immediately started causing problems by using unauthorized samples in their material, including from the Beals and Abba, which created all kinds of legal problems, which led them to travel to Sweden to try to negotiate with Abba. When that didn't work, they burned the remaining offending records in the field and through the rest overboard into the North Sea as they took the ferry home. Unchastened, they continued to infringe copyrights, the mission and possible theme, material from Whitney Houston and others, and after a few more months, the Jams were brought to an end."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
